reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A rare autoimmune blistering disease characterised by intraepidermal IgG-negative, IgA-mediated intercellular deposition
Presents with flaccid vesicles and pustules, often coalescing into annular or herpetiform patterns with central crusting on the trunk and flexures
Two main subtypes are recognised: the subcorneal pustular dermatosis (SPD) type and the intraepidermal neutrophilic (IEN) type, differing in the level of pustule formation
Desmocollin-1 is the principal target antigen in the SPD type, distinguishing it from classic desmoglein-driven pemphigus
Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgA deposition within the epidermis, the diagnostic hallmark
Pruritus is frequently prominent, and mucosal involvement is uncommon
Dapsone is often effective, reflecting the neutrophil-rich nature of the infiltrate; associations with monoclonal gammopathy and inflammatory bowel disease are reported
reference.pathophysiology: IgA pemphigus is driven by IgA autoantibodies directed against desmosomal cell-adhesion molecules, most characteristically desmocollin-1 in the subcorneal pustular dermatosis type and less well-defined desmosomal antigens in the intraepidermal neutrophilic type. IgA binding at the keratinocyte surface recruits neutrophils and promotes loss of intercellular adhesion, producing sterile pustules and mild acantholysis at either a subcorneal or a mid-epidermal level. The neutrophil-predominant inflammation underlies the clinical pustulation and the frequent responsiveness to dapsone. Circulating IgA intercellular antibodies may be detectable, and the condition can be associated with gammopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Dermatitis herpetiformis and linear IgA bullous dermatosis
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy for histology showing intraepidermal pustules with neutrophils and slight acantholysis
Direct immunofluorescence demonstrating intercellular IgA deposition
Indirect immunofluorescence for circulating IgA intercellular antibodies
Antigen-specific testing for anti-desmocollin-1 where available
Serum protein electrophoresis to screen for monoclonal gammopathy
Investigations for associated inflammatory bowel disease when clinically suggested
redFlags: Extensive pustulation with systemic upset requiring exclusion of pustular psoriasis or infection
Detection of an underlying monoclonal gammopathy needing haematological assessment
Secondary bacterial infection of eroded pustular skin
Poor response to therapy prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: IgA pemphigus generally follows a more benign and chronic course than classic pemphigus, frequently responding to dapsone, though relapses occur and any associated gammopathy requires ongoing monitoring.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the disease as subcorneal pustular dermatosis without performing direct immunofluorescence
Assuming desmoglein antibodies are present when desmocollin is the relevant target
Confusing sterile pustules with infection and treating with antibiotics alone
management: Use dapsone as first-line therapy, exploiting its suppression of the neutrophilic inflammation that drives the pustules
Add topical or systemic corticosteroids for disease control, with acitretin an option particularly in the subcorneal pustular dermatosis type
Consider colchicine or sulfapyridine as adjunctive or steroid-sparing agents in resistant disease
Screen for G6PD deficiency before dapsone and monitor for haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia during treatment
Manage pruritus and provide wound care for eroded pustules
Screen for and monitor an associated monoclonal gammopathy and investigate for inflammatory bowel disease when suggested
Follow up for relapse and taper therapy to the minimum needed to maintain remission

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of IgA pemphigus

nodes.text: Flaccid vesicles and pustules forming annular or herpetiform patterns on trunk
Extensive pustulation with systemic upset, or infection of eroded skin?
Exclude pustular psoriasis or infection; treat secondary infection
Skin biopsy, direct and indirect immunofluorescence, anti-desmocollin-1, SPEP
Intercellular IgA deposition confirmed on immunofluorescence?
Consider subcorneal pustular dermatosis or pustular psoriasis; repeat tests
Corticosteroids for control; acitretin in SPD type
Colchicine or sulfapyridine for resistant disease
Screen for monoclonal gammopathy; taper to lowest effective dose
Relapses possible; taper therapy to a remission-maintaining dose
